x-e-fill-02.title: When the poster and the school notebook differ
x-e-fill-02.topic: Fixing a contradiction between two notices
x-e-fill-02.goal: Compare two notices line by line, sort out what is a real contradiction from what only looks like one, and ask in English which is right.
x-e-fill-02.material:
The announcement of the school book fair is posted in two places (written in text only, without pictures).

[Hallway poster]
Book Fair
Friday
10 a.m. - 2 p.m.
Place: the gym

[Our class notebook]
Class 4-2: We will go to the Book Fair on Friday at 1 p.m. The Book Fair is in the library. Bring 3,000 won.
x-e-fill-02.thinking.0: Pairing the same items (day, time, place) in the two texts and comparing them
x-e-fill-02.thinking.1: Checking whether a time falls inside a time range
x-e-fill-02.thinking.2: Asking the right person in order to resolve the contradiction
x-e-fill-02.prereq.1: School words such as gym, library
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.prompt: Which item in the two notices does not match?
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.hint.0: Pair up the day, time, and place line by line and compare them.
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.hint.1: For the time, check not whether they are 'the same' but whether it falls 'inside' the poster's time range.
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.r.a: Put the words that give the day in the two texts side by side and check whether they are the same.
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.r.b: If you compare where each text says the book display is, they are different.
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.r.c: Check whether the notebook's 1 p.m. falls within the hours the poster says it is open.
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.o.d: There is no item that does not match
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.r.d: Look back and ask whether you read the 'Place' line and the 'in the ...' sentence to the end.
x-e-fill-02.s.s1.explain: The day is Friday in both. The notebook's 1 p.m. falls within the poster's 10 a.m.-2 p.m., so it is not a contradiction. The place is the gym on the poster and the library in the notebook, so they differ.
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences in English to your homeroom teacher and ask which one is right.
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write the place the poster says in one sentence.
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.hint.1: In the second sentence, say the place from the notebook and ask with 'Which ...?' or 'Where ...?'.
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write both places the two notices give?
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is there a question asking which place is right?
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid making an issue of the time, which is not a contradiction?
x-e-fill-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: A good question that shows the two candidates directly in the form 'A or B?'.

x-e-fill-03.title: Lucy's two requests: which one needs a question?
x-e-fill-03.topic: Judging whether the information is enough, and asking
x-e-fill-03.goal: Sort out which of two requests has enough information to help and which does not, and write in English the question needed for the one that lacks it.
x-e-fill-03.material:
Your pen pal Lucy sent two messages. Your town has two stations, Central Station and North Station.

[Message A] "Can you help me choose a birthday present for my brother? He is 8. He likes soccer. I can spend $20."

[Message B] "Can you meet me at the station tomorrow? I will bring the book."
x-e-fill-03.thinking.0: Judging whether you can start the job with the information already given
x-e-fill-03.thinking.1: Pointing out exactly what information is missing and asking for it
x-e-fill-03.prereq.0: Request expressions such as Can you ...?
x-e-fill-03.prereq.1: Easy words such as station, birthday present
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.prompt: Which message can you not help with unless you ask more?
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.hint.0: In each message, mark beside the line whether 'for whom / what / how much' or 'where / what time' is there.
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count only the things you really need to start helping.
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.r.a: Count whether A has all of the age, what he likes, and the money that can be spent.
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.r.b: Check whether B lets you know where and at what time to meet.
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.r.c: Think about whether A is really missing information that is truly needed to start choosing a present.
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.o.d: I can help right away with both messages
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.r.d: See whether you can tell from the sentence which of the two stations 'the station' in B means.
x-e-fill-03.s.s1.explain: A has the age (8), what he likes (soccer), and the budget ($20), so you can start choosing a present. In B, you cannot tell which of the two stations or what time, so you have to ask.
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.prompt: Reply in English to Lucy's message B. Ask for the information you really need in order to meet.
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.hint.0: To meet, you need both 'where' and 'what time'.
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.hint.1: It is clearer if you put in the names Central Station and North Station when you ask.
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you ask both which station and what time?
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid asking again about 'the book', which was already given?
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write it short and clear so Lucy can understand?
x-e-fill-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that asks 'Where and when' and gives the two station names directly.

x-e-fill-04.title: Asking Ben again after he dodged the question
x-e-fill-04.topic: Writing a question to ask for information missing from a conversation
x-e-fill-04.goal: Find the answer in a conversation that does not really answer the question, and ask again in an English question about the information you still do not know.
x-e-fill-04.material: This is a conversation between Mia and Ben. They are going to a newly opened indoor climbing gym.
x-e-fill-04.thinking.0: Pairing questions with answers and checking whether an answer actually came
x-e-fill-04.thinking.1: Turning information you do not yet know into questions
x-e-fill-04.prereq.0: Question expressions such as How much, What time
x-e-fill-04.prereq.1: The meanings of open, close, discount
x-e-fill-04.s.s1.hint.0: Pair one of Mia's questions with Ben's answer right after it.
x-e-fill-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether specific information such as a number or a time came out in the answer.
x-e-fill-04.s.s1.explain: Line 3 only says 'there is a discount' to a question asking the price (how much), and does not say how much. Line 5 is not an answer to whether it is open all day, but a remark that the place is fun. Whichever of the two lines you choose is correct.
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.prompt: Write the English question Mia will send to Ben again. Ask about all the information you still do not know.
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.hint.0: You can also split price and time into separate sentences, one each.
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.hint.1: You can put words for asking again at the front, like 'Sorry, but ...'.
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you ask about both things, the price and the time?
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid asking again about what was already answered (that there is a discount)?
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it a polite and natural question?
x-e-fill-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: Another way of saying it using price/until.
x-e-fill-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose one of Ben's answers that does not give the information needed for the question Mia asked. (Even if several lines apply, you only need to choose one of them.)

x-e-fill-05.title: Rewriting a club notice so nobody misunderstands
x-e-fill-05.goal: Find the ambiguous parts in an English instruction that can be read in several ways, and rewrite it as a notice no one can misunderstand, using the given facts.
x-e-fill-05.thinking.0: Finding unclear words in an instruction (where, when, how much)
x-e-fill-05.thinking.1: Putting in the facts so it can be read only one way
x-e-fill-05.prereq.0: Basic words such as bring, before, meeting
x-e-fill-05.prereq.1: English expressions for days and times
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each word of the notice, ask yourself, 'What exactly is that?'
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.r.a: Check whether you can tell which room it is from inside the notice sentence.
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.r.c: Check whether the notice alone tells you which day of that week and what time.
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.r.d: Check whether the sentence tells you how much, and what the money is for.
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.hint.1: Keep the original sentence as a frame and swap in the specific information one piece at a time.
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid leaving out the items in the original notice (form, costume)?
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Could even a brand-new member read it and act right away?
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer made easy to read by splitting it into two sentences.
x-e-fill-05.material:
The drama club teacher put up the notice below.

"Please bring the form, your costume, and the money to the room before the meeting next week."

[Facts] The meeting is on Wednesday at 4 p.m., and the meeting place is Room 204. The money to pay is 3,000 won for a ticket. The form and the costume were decided at the last meeting, so everyone already knows them (the form is one sheet, and the costume is one hat that each person has).
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions in the notice that different readers could understand differently. (Things that [Facts] says everyone already knows count as not ambiguous.)
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each expression in the notice, mark whether [Facts] has new information that tells it (a room number, a day and time, an amount, etc.).
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.r.b: Look at whether [Facts] shows that the costume is already known to everyone.
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.r.e: Look for whether [Facts] shows that the form is already known to everyone.
x-e-fill-05.s.s1.explain: You cannot tell which room "the room" is, what day and time "next week" is, or how much "the money" is. "The form" and "your costume" were decided at the last meeting and everyone already knows them, so there is almost no chance of misunderstanding.
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.prompt: Using the information in [Facts], rewrite the notice in one or two English sentences so that all three items of the original notice (the form, the costume, and the money) are included and there is no misunderstanding.
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.hint.0: For each expression you chose as ambiguous in s1, find the matching information in [Facts].
x-e-fill-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you change all the ambiguous expressions (room, time, amount) into specific ones?

x-e-fill-06.title: The hidden meaning of a short memo changes as you read more
x-e-fill-06.topic: Inferring intention and mood from clues in a short text
x-e-fill-06.goal: As a short memo is revealed bit by bit, infer the writer's intention, and when a new clue appears, change your judgment and explain it by quoting the clues.
x-e-fill-06.material: A senior colleague (the manager) sent a memo to the new hire Sam. We will reveal it one sentence at a time. It is the day after Sam handed in a report.
x-e-fill-06.thinking.0: Checking and changing your first judgment each time a clue is added
x-e-fill-06.thinking.1: Telling praise expressions apart from indirect requests
x-e-fill-06.thinking.2: Quoting from the text the expressions your judgment was based on
x-e-fill-06.prereq.0: Easy expressions such as thanks, next time, maybe
x-e-fill-06.prereq.1: A basic understanding of speaking indirectly
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.prompt: Read the memo little by little and judge the writer's intention.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.hint.0: Judge only from the sentences you can see now. Do not decide ahead of time what will come later.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: From the text seen so far, what is the most suitable intention?
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.0.after: From this one sentence alone, it is most natural to see it as praise.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judged from only one sentence. It is reasonable now, but it may change with later text.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Look for a clue of criticism in 'Nice work'.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Look for words related to a schedule.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: A sentence has been added. What is the most suitable judgment?
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.after: The praise is about time and effort, and there is not yet any word that the content of the report is good. Remember that the evaluation of the result is still empty.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Tell apart whether the praise is about 'time' and 'staying late', or about the result.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It recognizes the effort but does not yet evaluate the result
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a judgment that reads effort and result separately.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: A text written in anger at Sam
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Look for words that show anger.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: You have read all of it. What is the most suitable judgment?
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.after: The earlier praise is about effort, and 'Next time, maybe start from the template' and 'Come see me' are indirect requests to fix this report.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Praise that admits the whole result is excellent
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Think about whether 'Next time' and 'template' fit with praise.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: An indirect request that recognizes effort and asks for a fix
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Look at what role 'maybe' and 'Next time' play after the praise.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.reflect: At first it looked like praise, but each time a new sentence appeared you looked at 'what is being praised' and changed your judgment. Say that a judgment can change when clues are added.
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.prompt: Explain the reason by quoting two or more expressions from the memo that your final judgment was based on. (In Korean or English)
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.hint.0: First find one sentence that made your judgment change.
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.hint.1: Put that sentence next to the first praise sentence and explain.
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you quote praise expressions and request expressions separately?
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain that 'the praise is about effort'?
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you give evidence without deciding that the writer is angry?
x-e-fill-06.s.s2.model.0: "I'm sure it took a lot of time" recognizes only the effort and says nothing about the result. "Next time, maybe start from the template" is an indirect way of telling Sam to fix this report, so it is a polite request for a fix.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each sentence that gives praise, look at what it praises and whether the thing praised is the same.
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A text written by someone sure that the content of the report is perfect
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: A notice that the next report will be left to someone else
x-e-fill-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The memo says nothing about leaving it to someone else. Look at what "Come see me" means together with the other sentences.

x-e-fill-07.title: When the numbers in the news and the annual report differ
x-e-fill-07.topic: Finding where two sources' numbers disagree and asking a question to resolve it
x-e-fill-07.goal: Reconcile the numbers of two sources by calculation to find where they match and where they differ, choose the possibilities that could explain the difference, and write in English a question to the library to resolve it.
x-e-fill-07.material:
These are two sources about the city library's usage in 2023.

[Source A: news article] "The city library had 13,200 visitors in 2023, up 10%."

[Source B: the library's annual report] "2022: 12,000 visits. 2023: 13,500 visits (up 12.5%)."
x-e-fill-07.thinking.0: Working backward from a percentage to the earlier value to compare two sources
x-e-fill-07.thinking.1: Comparing and evaluating the possibilities that could create the difference
x-e-fill-07.thinking.2: Making a question that resolves the difference
x-e-fill-07.prereq.0: Working backward from a percentage increase to find the earlier value
x-e-fill-07.prereq.1: Words such as visits, visitors, annual report
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.prompt: When you reconcile the numbers of the two sources by calculation, what can you tell?
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.o.a: Both the 2022 figure and the rate of increase differ, and only the 2023 figure is the same
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.r.a: Read the numbers again to check which side's 2023 figure is the same.
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.o.b: The 2023 figure is the same, but the 2022 figure and the rate of increase differ from each other
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.r.b: Compare B's 2023 figure and A's 2023 figure side by side.
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.o.c: When calculated, all the figures and the rates of increase are the same, so nothing is off
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.r.c: Check whether 13,200 and 13,500, and 10% and 12.5%, are really the same.
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.o.d: When calculated, 2022 is the same, and the 2023 figure and the rate of increase differ from each other
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment made by calculating what 2022 would have to be for a 10% increase to become 13,200.
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.explain: A says 13,200 with a 10% increase, so 2022 is 13,200÷1.10=12,000. This is the same as B's 2022 figure of 12,000. But for 2023, A has 13,200 and B has 13,500, and the rates of increase also differ: 10% and 12.5% (13,500÷12,000=1.125).
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose every possibility that could actually explain the difference in the 2023 figures (13,200 and 13,500).
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.hint.0: If each explanation were true, think about which number would get bigger or smaller.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare again the words A and B used (visitors, visits) and the periods.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.o.b: One counted up to the end of December, and the other counted up to the end of November
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.r.b: Think about whether numbers can differ if the counting period is different.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.o.d: One counted the number of people who visited, and the other counted the number of visits
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.r.d: Compare the words A and B used: visitors and visits.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.o.e: One side corrected its number, but the other side used the value from before the correction
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.r.e: Think about whether the two sources are values from the same point in time.
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.prompt: Write an English question to send to the library in one or two sentences. Include both numbers, and ask in a way that lets you check the cause of the difference.
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.hint.0: First write the names of the two sources (news, report) and the numbers side by side.
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.hint.1: Then turn one of the causes you chose in s2 into a question.
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you quote both numbers exactly?
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you ask about the cause without deciding that one side is wrong?
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you ask specifically about the counting period or the way of counting?
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: A question that presents the two numbers as 'A or B?' and asks about the difference in period.
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write side by side in a table the figures that overlap in the two sources (visits by year, rate of increase).
x-e-fill-07.s.s1.hint.1: Try to see whether a figure that appears in only one source can be calculated from the figures in the other source.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.o.a: A just rounded 13,500 and shortened it to 13,200
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.r.a: However you round 13,500, it does not become 13,200. A difference of 300 does not come from rounding, so check it for real.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.o.c: A wrote its figure for 2022, and B wrote its figure for 2023
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.r.c: Check again whether both sources wrote 2023.
x-e-fill-07.s.s2.explain: The counting period, the unit being counted (number of people versus number of visits), and the time of correction can all make a difference. Rounding cannot turn 13,500 into 13,200, and both sources give figures for 2023.
x-e-fill-07.s.s3.modelNote.2: A question that asks about the time of correction.

x-e-fill-08.title: The hidden meaning of a reference letter with only praise
x-e-fill-08.topic: Inferring implied meaning and hidden intention
x-e-fill-08.goal: Use both what is written and what is not written in a reference letter as clues to infer the hidden evaluation, and write in English a strong recommendation that fills in what was missing.
x-e-fill-08.material:
Daniel applied for a research assistant position analyzing data. This is part of a reference letter (fictional) written by his former boss.

"Daniel is always punctual, he is polite to everyone, and he keeps a very tidy desk. I am sure he will be happy in whatever job he finds."
x-e-fill-08.thinking.0: Using both what is written and what is missing as clues
x-e-fill-08.thinking.1: Finding and fixing a leap with no evidence
x-e-fill-08.thinking.2: Writing yourself what makes a difference
x-e-fill-08.prereq.0: Words such as recommend, punctual, tidy
x-e-fill-08.prereq.1: Knowing roughly what kind of text a reference letter is
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.prompt: What is the best-supported hidden evaluation by this writer?
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.hint.0: Look for whether the text has the ability that matters most for the position applied for.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write down separately the praise that is in the text and the praise that is not.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.r.a: For a data analysis position, look at what kind of content is written and what kind is not.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.r.b: Check whether the letter talks about abilities directly related to the position applied for.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.r.c: Look for negative words in the sentences.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that what is not written is a clue.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.explain: All the praise is about work attitude (being on time, politeness, tidiness), and data analysis or research ability never appears. The last sentence also says 'whatever job' instead of this position, which hints that the confidence is weak. However, it is not 'certain', only a hint.
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.prompt: A student interpreted this letter as below. Which line contains a leap with no evidence?
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.hint.0: Line by line, tell apart what is actually written in the text from what is not written.
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find which line states something not in the text as if it were a fact.
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.line.1: Therefore it means Daniel is also excellent at data analysis.
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.prompt: Write two English sentences that a writer who strongly recommends Daniel for the same position would write. Include evidence of a specific ability related to the position that was not in the original letter.
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.hint.0: Think again about what was missing from the letter.
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one thing 'the person did himself' and write it starting with a verb.
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write evidence of a specific ability (something he did) that was not in the original letter?
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is that evidence related to the position applied for (data analysis research assistant)?
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does the feeling of recommending come through clearly?
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that gives a specific task (designing an experiment) and its result.
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.o.a: It merely records Daniel's personality and habits as facts, with no special meaning
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.o.b: It thinks highly of Daniel's analytical ability and strongly recommends him for this position
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.o.c: It tells us that Daniel's personality is bad and that he is hard to work with
x-e-fill-08.s.s1.o.d: It praises only his work attitude and does not mention the abilities the position needs, which hints that the writer is not very confident
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.line.0: The praise in the recommendation letter is about work attitude, such as punctual, polite, and tidy.
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.line.2: The writer did not directly say that he recommends Daniel for this position.
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.line.3: "I am sure" in the last sentence expresses the writer's personal opinion.
x-e-fill-08.s.s2.explain: Line 2 asserted that Daniel has analytical ability, which is not in the letter. Line 1 summarized the praise written in the letter, line 3 correctly pointed out something that is missing from the letter, and line 4 correctly read the nature of the expression.
x-e-fill-08.s.s3.modelNote.2: It gave a strong recommendation using only concrete evidence, without a recommending word.
